land: National Park Service areas (national parks, seashores, and monuments the NPS manages)
rule: Except as the chapter provides otherwise, possessing or using a metal detector is prohibited. Exceptions include a device broken down and stored or packed to prevent its use, and one used for authorized scientific, mining or administrative work.

land: Bureau of Land Management public lands
rule: Reasonable amounts of rocks, mineral specimens and semiprecious gemstones may be collected for noncommercial purposes. This does not apply on developed recreation sites and areas, or where a posted rule prohibits it. Explosive, motorized or mechanical devices may not be used to collect them, except metal detectors.

land: Bureau of Land Management public lands (mining rules)
rule: In the BLM mining rules, casual use means activities that ordinarily cause no or negligible disturbance. It generally includes hand panning, non-motorized sluicing and metal detectors used to sense the presence of minerals.

land: Bureau of Land Management public lands
rule: Unless otherwise authorized, willfully defacing, disturbing, removing or destroying any personal property, structure, or scientific, cultural, archaeological or historic resource is prohibited.

land: Bureau of Land Management public lands
rule: The BLM can issue an order that temporarily closes designated public lands or restricts their use. It posts the order at its office, near or within the area, through local media and online.

land: Federal public lands and Indian lands
rule: Excavating, removing, damaging or defacing an archaeological resource, or trying to, is prohibited without a permit or a listed exemption. A knowing violation is a federal crime.

land: Federal public lands and Indian lands
rule: An item is an archaeological resource under ARPA only if it is at least 100 years old.

land: Federal public lands and Indian lands
rule: Coins, bullets and unworked minerals and rocks are not archaeological resources unless found in a direct physical relationship with archaeological resources.
Digging in, disturbing or removing any prehistoric, historic or archaeological resource is prohibited.

land: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers lakes and projects
rule: Metal detectors are permitted on designated beaches or other previously disturbed areas unless the District Commander prohibits them to protect archaeological, historical or paleontological resources. The Manager's Office has the metal detector policy and designated use areas.

land: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers lakes and projects
rule: Found items must be handled under 36 CFR 327.15 and 327.16, except non-identifiable items such as coins worth less than $25.

The United States asserts title to certain abandoned shipwrecks and transfers it to the state whose submerged lands hold them. Wrecks on federal public lands belong to the United States, and wrecks on Indian lands to the tribe that owns the land.

land: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers lakes and projects
rule: Removing or altering public property, historical and archaeological features included, is prohibited except with the District Commander's written permission.

Except as the chapter provides otherwise, possessing, destroying, injuring, defacing, removing, digging or disturbing cultural or archeological resources, paleontological specimens or mineral resources is prohibited.
Damaging or removing any natural feature or other property of the United States is prohibited.
No one may remove, injure or destroy any object of archaeological or historical interest or value.

The Gold Fields District order for Folsom Lake SRA is dated Jan. 1, 2022. It cites 14 CCR 4301(i), 4307, 4308 and 4326 and Public Resources Code 5003 and 5008. It shows a district restricting detectors in one park unit.

land: Folsom Lake State Recreation Area, California
rule: Possessing or using a metal detector is prohibited. The listed exemptions are carrying one unused in a vehicle on a public road and a permit under 43 CFR 423.50. The district superintendent can also grant a written exception.

Destroying, disturbing, mutilating or removing earth, sand, gravel, oil, minerals, rocks, paleontological features or features of caves is prohibited. Rockhounding may be permitted as defined in 14 CCR 4301(v).

No one may destroy, injure, move, dig, harmfully disturb or remove listed items from a park area. The list covers buildings, structures, historic ruins, soil, sand, gravel, rocks, minerals, artifacts and other materials.

land: Land owned or controlled by the state of Florida
rule: Removing or disturbing an archaeological site or specimen on state-owned or state-controlled land without a permit is prohibited.
Except for park personnel, law enforcement and utilities, using a metal detector is prohibited in all Kentucky state parks.
Only park personnel, law enforcement and utilities may use metal detectors there.
The stated purpose is to preclude unnecessary damage to natural areas and other facilities. It also aims to run efficient, orderly parks for the great number of visitors.
The text was last certified effective Feb. 12, 2020, and lists a 7-year expiration date of Feb. 12, 2027.

land: New York, Long Island state parks
rule: Metal detecting is allowed by permit only, in designated areas of listed parks. Jones Beach, Sunken Meadow, Hither Hills, Montauk Point, Napeague, Orient Beach, Valley Stream and Wildwood are among them.
citation: NYS Parks, Long Island Region Metal Detecting Permit Guide

land: New York, Long Island state parks
rule: The permit costs $40 a year and expires December 31.
citation: NYS Parks, Long Island Region Metal Detecting Permit Guide

land: New York, Long Island state parks
rule: In designated areas, by permit only, no digging tool may be larger than 1.5 in wide by 6 in long. Dug ground must be restored at once.
citation: NYS Parks, Long Island Region Metal Detecting Permit Guide

land: New York, Long Island state parks
rule: Items worth more than $20 and any archaeological artifact go to Park Police.
citation: NYS Parks, Long Island Region Metal Detecting Permit Guide

land: New York, Long Island state parks
rule: Beach dune areas, golf courses, driving ranges, residences and landscaped areas are off limits. Detecting must not interfere with wildlife and piping plover nesting areas.
citation: NYS Parks, Long Island Region Metal Detecting Permit Guide

land: New York state parks (property of the state parks office)
rule: Making an excavation on, or injuring, defacing, removing or tampering with, any real or personal property, tree or other plant life is absolutely prohibited.

land: New York, Long Island state parks
rule: The permit maps mark some designated areas as open year-round and others as open only from Memorial Day to Labor Day.
citation: NYS Parks, Long Island Region Metal Detecting Permit Guide

land: New York, Central Region state parks
rule: A $10 permit allows a metal detector in the sandy beach area only of listed parks, in daylight. It runs from Jan. 1 to May 15 and from the Tuesday after Labor Day to Dec. 31. Coins may be kept; other finds go to the park office.
citation: NYS Parks, Central Region Metal Detector Permit

land: New York, Saratoga-Capital District state parks
rule: A $10 permit allows detecting in the designated beach areas of Moreau Lake, Grafton Lakes, Cherry Plain and Thompsons Lake, only outside the swimming season. Detectors are prohibited in all NYS Historic Sites.
citation: NYS Parks, Saratoga-Capital District Metal Detector Permit

rule: Metal detectors are not allowed in any state park area. The one exception is finding lost personal property, with a Special Use Permit from the park superintendent or a designee.

land: North Carolina beaches outside state parks
rule: Local ordinances may govern metal detecting on beaches that are not state parks; NC DEQ says to contact the beach town.
Ask permission from the forest supervisor of the forest you want to search.

land: North Carolina inland lakes and beaches
rule: Ask the property owner for permission to use a metal detector.
No permit from NC DEQ is needed, but the landowner’s permission is required before you go on the property.
The NC Department of Natural and Cultural Resources may have its own rules on metal detecting, particularly in historic areas.

land: Ohio state parks (Division of Parks and Watercraft)
rule: Metal detecting is allowed on sand beaches and mowed areas, except mowed areas of golf courses, rental facilities and campgrounds.
Any disturbed ground must be returned at once to a condition as close to undisturbed as possible.
Detecting anywhere else needs written permission from the area manager.

land: Oregon ocean shore state recreation area
rule: Metal detecting needs no written permit in the areas on OPRD’s "Detecting Allowed" list.
Anywhere not on the "Detecting Allowed" list, a special use permit or the park manager’s written permission is required.

land: Oregon ocean shore state recreation area
rule: No one may dig up or remove sand, soil, rock, historical or fossil materials without the department's written permission. Sections 3 and 4 make exceptions for tribal members and small personal-use amounts. Disturbing an archaeological site needs a permit.
At any park property, or part of one, not on the "Detecting Allowed" list, using a metal detector needs written permission. It comes from the park manager or a designated employee.

Digging up or removing sand, soil, rock, historical or fossil materials needs written permission from a designated park employee. Excavating or removing archaeological or historical objects needs the director's authorization.

land: Oregon ocean shore, western snowy plover occupied sites
rule: All recreation is restricted within the demarked dry sand areas from March 15 to September 15. The department may end the restrictions on July 15 if nesting stops.
Operating or using a metal detector in a state park is an offense unless a permit authorizes it.
Metal detectors may be used only on designated manmade beaches, and only with a DCR special use permit obtained from the park's manager.
citation: Virginia State Parks rule, quoted by DHR

land: State and federal land in Virginia
rule: Public property, state and federal, is generally not open to metal detecting and removal of artifacts, with a few exceptions. DHR adds that, contrary to what some hobby websites say, Virginia has no general permitting process for metal detecting.

land: State-owned bottoms of Virginia's rivers, the Chesapeake Bay and the Atlantic coastal zone
rule: Underwater historic property on the state-owned bottom belongs to the Commonwealth. Any recovery that removes, destroys or disturbs it needs a permit from the Virginia Marine Resources Commission first. A violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor.
Detecting on private property needs the owner's permission. DHR warns that detecting without it can lead to charges of trespass and theft.
Some counties allow metal detecting on manmade beaches or around sports fields. Each county's parks and recreation department says if and where.
Metal detecting is allowed only in posted areas of approved state parks and in approved campsites, during posted open daylight hours. Approved campsites are the user's own or unoccupied ones.
You must register with park staff at the park before detecting.

In the posted detecting areas, digging tools are limited to ice picks, screwdrivers and probes no wider than 2 in. Sand scoops may be no larger than 6 in wide by 8 in long, with perforations at least 1/2 in wide, and only on sand. Holes may be no deeper than 6 in and are refilled at once, with the surface restored.
Anything that is or appears to be of historical or archaeological significance stays where it was found. It must be reported to park staff at once, and the area of the find is then closed.
The rule permits metal detecting and the removal of small contemporary materials in state parks the director or a designee selects.
Detecting is not allowed during seasonal or emergency park closures, except where posted. Exceptional uses may be approved through a special recreation event application.
A violation of the metal detector rule is an infraction under chapter 7.84 RCW.
